title: Quantization for Inference
interviewAnswer: Quantization represents weights and sometimes activations with fewer bits—such as INT8 or 4-bit—to reduce memory, bandwidth and often latency. Post-training quantization is simpler; quantization-aware training can preserve quality when aggressive quantization hurts accuracy.
why: Large models are often memory-bandwidth bound, so fewer bits can be the difference between one GPU and several GPUs.
intuition: Instead of storing every parameter as a 32-bit float, approximate values using a smaller discrete set plus scale/zero-point information.
deepDive: Symmetric/asymmetric schemes trade implementation simplicity and range. Calibration estimates activation ranges for PTQ. LLM weight-only quantization can dramatically reduce memory, but kernel/hardware support determines actual speedup.
workedExample: A 7B-parameter model is roughly 28 GB just for FP32 weights, ~14 GB at FP16, and around 3.5–7 GB for 4–8-bit weights before runtime overhead.
commonMistakes: Assuming smaller model files guarantee faster inference.
Reporting quantization without rechecking task quality and long-tail failures.
followUps: Why might INT8 be slower on unsupported hardware?
production: Choose quantization by measured memory/latency/quality on target hardware; keep a higher-precision fallback for critical workloads.

lab.goal: Compare dynamic INT8 quantization with the FP32 module on CPU.
lab.buildIt:
import torch
m=torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(128,256),torch.nn.ReLU(),torch.nn.Linear(256,10)).eval()
x=torch.randn(32,128); y_fp=m(x)
q=torch.ao.quantization.quantize_dynamic(m,{torch.nn.Linear},dtype=torch.qint8)
y_q=q(x); print((y_fp-y_q).abs().mean().item())
lab.useIt:
import io
b1=io.BytesIO(); b2=io.BytesIO(); torch.save(m.state_dict(),b1); torch.save(q.state_dict(),b2)
print('bytes fp32/int8',len(b1.getvalue()),len(b2.getvalue()))
